name: Mongol Empire
era: 1206 to 1368, and a living steppe culture
line: Travel light, keep your word, open your door and look to the sky.

quote.text: If, like the five arrow-shafts, each of you keeps to himself, you can easily be broken by anyone. If you are together and of one mind, like the bound arrow-shafts, how can anyone easily break you?
quote.by: Alan the Fair, to her five sons
quote.source: The Secret History of the Mongols, section 22, after the translation of Igor de Rachewiltz

quotes.text: We have no friend but our shadow, we have no whip but our horse’s tail.
quotes.source: The Secret History of the Mongols, sections 76 to 78, after the translation of Igor de Rachewiltz

quotes.text: I hate luxury and exercise moderation. I have only one coat and one food. I eat the same food and am dressed in the same tatters as my humble herdsmen.
quotes.source: Letter summoning the Daoist master Changchun, 1219, trans. E. Bretschneider, 1888

quotes.text: Just as God gave different fingers to the hand so has He given different ways to men.
quotes.source: To the friar William of Rubruck at Karakorum, 1254, in Rubruck’s report, trans. in Christopher Dawson, The Mongol Mission

quotes.text: From the rising of the sun to its setting, all the lands have been made subject to me.
quotes.source: Letter to Pope Innocent IV, 1246, trans. in Christopher Dawson, The Mongol Mission

quotes.text: They came, they sapped, they burnt, they slew, they plundered and they departed.
quotes.by: A survivor of the sack of Bukhara
quotes.source: Reported by Juvaini, The History of the World Conqueror, about 1260, trans. J. A. Boyle

quotes.text: The empire was won on horseback, but it cannot be governed on horseback.
quotes.source: His advice to Ögedei Khan, as recorded in the Chinese History of the Yuan

words.usage: The highest power. Older texts write Tengri. The Mongols prayed to the Eternal Blue Sky and believed it had given them the earth to rule.
The phrase that opened every imperial decree: by the strength of the Eternal Sky.
The lord of a people. The supreme ruler was the khagan, the great khan.
A lattice wall and roof poles covered in felt, put up in an hour and warm at forty below. The door faces south. Russians call it a yurt.
A mobile palace of tents and carts. It gives English the word horde.
A council of princes and commanders that chose the khan and decided on war. Staying away meant opposition.
In Mongolian, Ikh Zasag, the great law. The rulings of Chinggis Khan on discipline, theft, the hunt and the sharing of spoils. No full text survives.
The maxims of Chinggis Khan, memorised and recited at gatherings.
In Mongolian, örtöö. Stations a day’s ride apart with fresh horses, food and lodging for couriers, across the whole empire.
In Mongolian, gerege. A metal passport that entitled the bearer to horses and supplies at every station.
One who has left his own clan to serve a leader of his choosing. Chinggis Khan built his army from them.
Two men who exchange gifts and an oath become closer than kin. Temüjin and Jamukha were anda, and then enemies.
First the people who follow a ruler, wherever they camp. Only later the land. Modern Mongolia calls itself Mongol Uls.
The largest unit of an army organised in tens, hundreds and thousands, which cut across the old tribes.
Ten thousand picked men who served the khan by day and night in turns. It was also the school of generals and governors.
A title given for great service, carrying freedom from tax and pardon for up to nine offences.
A spear hung with horsehair, white for peace and black for war. It held the soul and fortune of a leader.
One who speaks with the spirits of sky, earth and ancestors, with a drum and a costume hung with iron.
A heap of stones on a pass or hilltop. Travellers walk round it three times, with the sun, and add a stone.
Milk or tea flicked skywards with a carved wooden spoon, to the sky and the land, each morning and before a journey.
The fire at the centre of the ger. It is the family line itself. Nothing unclean goes into it.
The land a person belongs to, wherever they have been taken. A deep word in Mongolian songs.
The open grassland, a sea of it, from Hungary to Manchuria.
Children ride before they walk far. Each soldier took three or four remounts, which is how armies covered a hundred kilometres a day.
Lightly alcoholic and sour, churned in a hide bag by the door. The drink of summer. Turkic peoples call it kumis.
Milk, curds, cream, dried cheese. Pure and honoured, the food of summer, as meat is the food of winter.
The first of the three manly games. No weight classes and no time limit: whoever touches the ground first loses.
The gathering for wrestling, archery and horse racing, held since the empire and before.
A wrap-over coat belted with a sash, worn by men and women, cut for riding.
A winter of deep snow or ice that kills the herds. The steppe’s oldest fear.

practices.name: The morning offering to the sky
practices.instructions: As soon as you have made the first tea or opened the first milk of the day, take a small cup of it outside or to an open window. Face the rising sun. Flick a few drops upward to the sky, then to the four directions and to the earth. Say thank you for the day. Drink the rest. The rule of this Onda is to greet the sky first.
practices.why: On the steppe, the first of the milk or tea is offered to the sky, Tenger, and the earth. It is a small thanks that begins the day with humility.
variations: Use a spoonful of water if you have no tea.
Flick three drops with your ring finger.
Offer it to a tree.

practices.name: Cover ground
practices.instructions: Go a long way under the open sky today, further than is convenient, by your own effort or on an animal: walk, run, ride a horse or a bicycle. Leave the paths you know. Carry water and little else. As you go, read the landscape: wind, clouds, the shape of the land. Dress for the weather, tell someone where you are going and turn back before you are tired.
practices.why: The nomad’s life is a life of distance and horizons. Covering ground under the open sky is the most Mongol thing you can do.
variations: Walk thirty minutes if you have less time.
Cycle somewhere new.
Climb a hill to look at the horizon.

practices.name: Carry only what you need
practices.instructions: Before leaving the house, decide what you really need for the day and carry only that. Empty your pockets and bag of everything extra. Own what you can carry is a rule of this Onda. Notice how light you feel. Nomads moved camp twice a year with everything on carts and camels, and chose carefully what to keep.
practices.why: The Mongol rule of owning what you can carry is the root of the steppe’s freedom. Packing light is a daily practice of it.
variations: Leave your bag at home for a day.
Take only one book.
Empty a drawer of the unused.

practices.name: Look to the horizon
practices.instructions: Go to a window, balcony or open space and look at the farthest thing you can see for five minutes. Let your eyes rest on the horizon. Nomadic herders read the weather, the grass and the animals from far off. Give your eyes the relief of distance. Breathe slowly and notice what you see.
practices.why: Looking at distance is a restful practice for eyes and mind. On the steppe the horizon is the daily companion.
variations: Watch the clouds move.
Find the farthest tree.
Look at the sky after sunrise.

practices.name: Salted milk tea
practices.instructions: Make suutei tsai: boil water with a handful of green or black tea, add milk and a pinch of salt, and simmer until the colour is rich and creamy. Pour it into bowls and drink it hot, with bread or biscuits. It is the daily drink of Mongolia and the first thing offered to any visitor. Share a bowl.
practices.why: Suutei tsai, salty milk tea, is the heart of Mongolian hospitality. It warms the body on a cold steppe morning.
variations: Add rice or millet to make it a meal.
Offer a bowl to a neighbour.
Drink it with something fried.

practices.name: Greet a guest as a guest
practices.instructions: Greet each person you meet today as if they were a guest arriving at your tent, with a smile and a question after their health, their family and their animals. In Mongolia the greeting is a conversation: Sain baina uu? Are you well? Are your herds well? Take your time. Never rush a greeting.
practices.why: Steppe greetings are long and warm, because on the empty plain every meeting matters. A slow greeting is a gift.
variations: Learn sain baina uu.
Ask after someone’s family by name.
Offer the first greeting to a neighbour.

practices.name: One of the three games
practices.instructions: Train one of the three skills of the steppe for thirty minutes. Wrestling: grapple with a partner, or practise the stance, squats and lifts that wrestlers use. Archery: shoot at a target, or throw at one, with full attention. Riding: ride a horse or a bicycle, or practise balance. Never aim at a person or animal, warm up first and stop if anything hurts.
practices.why: Wrestling, archery and horse racing are the three manly games of Naadam, and the old skills of the steppe. Training one is a pleasure of its own.
variations: Throw darts or beanbags at a target.
Do balance exercises.
Cycle hard for half an hour.

practices.name: Keep an open door
practices.instructions: Today, feed whoever comes. Put the kettle on the moment anyone crosses your threshold, before you ask what they want. Offer the cup with your right hand, the left hand under your elbow. Give food with it, and the best of what you have. Nobody should leave a Mongolian tent hungry. The rule of this Onda is to feed the guest before you ask his business.
practices.why: Hospitality to travellers is a sacred duty on the steppe, where a stranger might die without shelter. The open door is the heart of nomad ethics.
variations: Put out a tea tray.
Invite a neighbour in.
Always say yes to a visitor.

practices.name: Your word is iron
practices.instructions: Make one promise today and keep it exactly. Be on time, do what you said you would, finish what you began. The Mongols prized the word of honour, and an oath was binding. If you cannot keep a promise, say so in advance. Say little, mean it all. The rule of this Onda is that your word is iron.
practices.why: Trustworthiness was the basis of trade and alliance on the steppe. A person’s word was their bond.
variations: Keep a promise you made long ago.
Be five minutes early.
Make fewer promises.

practices.name: Throw the shagai
practices.instructions: Play with shagai, sheep ankle bones, or any four small objects with different faces. Toss them and read the result: horse, sheep, camel or goat, according to the side that lands up. Shagai is used for games and for fortune-telling. Flick the bones across a table at targets, or divine a small decision. Use dice if you have no bones.
practices.why: Shagai are Mongolia’s most beloved game pieces, used for dozens of games. The sides are named for animals, and each throw tells a story.
variations: Play a flicking game with friends.
Divine your day with a throw.
Make shagai from clay.

practices.name: Share what you have
practices.instructions: Share something with a neighbour or friend today: a pot of food, a tool, a book. In the Mongol tradition the spoils are divided fairly, and the generous leader is the best leader. Give the best portion. Don’t wait to be asked. The rule of this Onda is to share the spoils.
practices.why: Sharing food and goods is basic to steppe life. A generous person is respected far more than a rich one.
variations: Share a meal with someone alone.
Lend a tool.
Give away something good.

practices.name: Read the weather
practices.instructions: Go outside and read the weather like a herder. Look at the clouds, feel the wind, smell the air, watch the birds. Predict what the next three hours will bring and write it down. Check at the end of the afternoon. Herders on the steppe read the sky every day to know when to move their herds. Dress for the weather.
practices.why: Weather-reading is an essential skill for nomads, whose survival depends on it. It is also a good exercise in attention.
variations: Use a barometer or phone afterwards.
Keep a weather diary.
Teach a child to read clouds.

practices.name: Tend the hearth
practices.instructions: End the day at a fire or a single flame. Tidy the space round it first. Sit with your household or alone and keep the flame for twenty minutes without a screen. Put nothing dirty into it. Tell one story from your family’s past or from the day. Don’t step over the fire or point your feet at it. Use a safe fire or a candle.
practices.why: The hearth is the centre of the Mongol home, to be treated with respect. Keeping a flame at the end of the day is the oldest evening ritual of all.
variations: Sit by a campfire if you can.
Light a candle in a bowl.
Tell a story from a grandparent.

practices.name: A story by the fire
practices.instructions: Tell or read a story from the Secret History of the Mongols: the boy Temujin and his friend Jamukha, the stolen horses or the childhood of the future Chinggis Khan. Tell it with gestures and voices, as a bard would. Let the listener ask questions. End with a proverb. It is an old way to pass the long evenings.
practices.why: The Secret History is the oldest Mongolian book, full of vivid scenes. Oral storytelling is still a pleasure on the steppe.
variations: Tell it by candlelight.
Read a section aloud.
Tell a story about your own childhood.

practices.name: Throat singing and horse-head fiddle
practices.instructions: Play a recording of Mongolian throat singing or the horse-head fiddle, the morin khuur, and listen with your eyes closed. In throat singing one voice makes two notes at once, a low drone and a whistling melody above. The fiddle is said to imitate a horse’s gallop and neigh. Let the sound carry you across the steppe.
practices.why: Khöömii, throat singing, and the morin khuur are the most characteristic sounds of Mongolia. Both are included in UNESCO’s list of intangible heritage.
variations: Listen to long songs instead.
Try a low drone yourself.
Look at a picture of the fiddle.

practices.name: Look at the stars
practices.instructions: Go outside after dark and look at the sky for a quarter of an hour. Find the Great Bear, which Mongolians call the Seven Elders, and the North Star. Tenger, the eternal blue sky, is the highest spirit of the steppe. Lie back if the ground is dry, and wrap up warm. Think of the herders under the same stars.
practices.why: Tenger, the sky, is the supreme power in Mongol belief. Stargazing on the steppe is spectacular, with no lights for miles.
variations: Find the pole star.
Count shooting stars.
Sit in silence for ten minutes.

practices.name: A game of shatar
practices.instructions: Play shatar, Mongolian chess, with a friend or family. It is close to chess, with a noyon (lord) in the place of a king and a bers (tiger) in the place of a queen. Learn the moves online and play a game. Wrestle with the clock and shake hands at the end. It is a favourite for long winter evenings.
practices.why: Shatar is Mongolia’s chess, played on winter evenings in the ger. It descends from the same ancient game as chess.
variations: Play a quick blitz game.
Teach a child.
Look up the pieces.

practices.name: Walk three times round
practices.instructions: Choose a tree, a cairn, a big stone or a post and walk three times round it clockwise, as Mongols circle the ovoo, a sacred pile of stones. Place a small stone or a sprig on it as you pass. Think of those who will travel tomorrow, and wish them a safe journey. End with a bow to the horizon.
practices.why: The ovoo is a cairn on a pass or hill, honoured by travellers, who circle it three times and add a stone. Walking round one is a lovely custom.
variations: Make your own cairn with garden stones.
Circle a tree in the park.
Add a stone for each wish.

practices.name: A small Naadam
practices.instructions: Hold a mini Naadam with friends in a park: three games. Wrestling, safe and friendly, with the first to touch the ground losing. Archery, with a soft target and a bow or beanbags. And a race on foot or by bike. Cheer every contestant, award a prize to everyone and share a meal and tea. Naadam is the national festival of Mongolia.
practices.why: Naadam, the Three Manly Games of wrestling, archery and horse racing, is the great summer festival of Mongolia. A small, friendly version is a joy.
variations: Add a throwing game with shagai.
Eat boiled dumplings afterwards.
Give out ribbon prizes.

practices.name: A day under the big sky
practices.instructions: Spend a day in the biggest open space near you, a moor, a beach, a field or a hilltop. Take a flask of tea, bread, cheese and a blanket. Walk, sit, watch the sky and the weather. Make a small offering of tea to the sky. Stay until the light changes. Dress for the conditions and tell someone where you are going.
practices.why: The Mongolian steppe is the largest open grassland in the world. A day in any wide space gives a taste of its feeling of freedom.
variations: Bring binoculars.
Leave your phone off.
Fly a kite.

immersePlan.name: Read from The Secret History
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of the oldest Mongol text, perhaps Temujin’s childhood or the story of the arrows. Retell it to someone.

immersePlan.name: Read Marco Polo on the Mongols
immersePlan.text: Read a few pages of Marco Polo’s account of Khubilai Khan’s court and the Mongol postal service. Notice what impresses him.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of The Horde
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Marie Favereau’s account of the Golden Horde as a system of trade and exchange. Note one surprise.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Story of the Weeping Camel
immersePlan.text: Watch the gentle 2003 film about a Gobi family, a rejected baby camel and a musician summoned to sing it a lullaby. It is moving and true to life.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Cave of the Yellow Dog
immersePlan.text: Watch the 2005 film about a nomad girl who finds a stray dog. Notice the daily routines of the ger.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Eagle Huntress
immersePlan.text: Watch the 2016 documentary on a thirteen-year-old Kazakh girl in western Mongolia who trains an eagle. The scenery is magnificent.

immersePlan.name: Listen to a Mongolian long song
immersePlan.text: Play a urtiin duu, a long song with long, soaring notes, sung by Norovbanzad. Close your eyes and picture the steppe.

immersePlan.name: Listen to throat singing
immersePlan.text: Play khöömii by a Mongolian ensemble. Listen for the two notes at once.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the morin khuur
immersePlan.text: Play a piece for the horse-head fiddle. Imagine the horses it describes.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Compendium of Chronicles
immersePlan.text: Look at the Persian miniatures made for the Mongol rulers of Iran, showing sieges, courts and daily life. Pick a scene.

immersePlan.name: Look at Khubilai Khan Hunting
immersePlan.text: Look at Liu Guandao’s scroll of the Great Khan on horseback with his hunting party. Find the falcon.

immersePlan.name: Look at a paiza
immersePlan.text: Look at a paiza, the metal tablet that gave a traveller the khan’s protection on the road. Think about what it meant.

immersePlan.name: Boil mutton on the bone
immersePlan.text: Boil mutton on the bone in salted water, and eat it with your hands, with a sharp knife, or use chicken. Share with others.

immersePlan.name: Make buuz
immersePlan.text: Steam dumplings of minced meat or vegetables with onion and garlic. They are the food of Tsagaan Sar. Eat them hot with tea.

immersePlan.name: Taste aaruul
immersePlan.text: Taste dried curds, hard and sour, the snack of the steppe. Suck on a piece slowly. Try dried cheese if you can’t find them.

immersePlan.name: Brew suutei tsai
immersePlan.text: Boil tea with milk and a pinch of salt. Serve it in bowls and share with someone.

immersePlan.name: Try a fermented milk drink
immersePlan.text: Airag is fermented mare’s milk. Try a cousin that is easy to find, such as kefir or ayran, cold and tangy. Sip it slowly.

immersePlan.name: Brew brick tea
immersePlan.text: Shave a little pressed tea from a brick and boil it. It is the tea of the steppe, strong and smoky. If you do not have a brick, use a strong black tea.

immersePlan.name: Step over the threshold, never on it
immersePlan.text: Today, step over the threshold of your home and of any place you enter, never on it. In Mongolia, the threshold is sacred. Notice how it slows you.

immersePlan.name: Pass things with the right hand
immersePlan.text: Offer and receive things today with your right hand, the left hand under the right elbow. It is the Mongolian gesture of respect.

immersePlan.name: Circle an ovoo
immersePlan.text: Walk three times clockwise round a tree or cairn and add a stone or sprig. Wish someone a safe journey.

immersePlan.name: Play shagai
immersePlan.text: Play with four ankle bones or dice, tossing them and naming the animal on each side. Play a flicking game with friends.

immersePlan.name: Watch bökh wrestling
immersePlan.text: Watch a bout of Mongolian wrestling, with the dance of the eagle before and after. Notice the ritual and the respect.

immersePlan.name: Play shatar
immersePlan.text: Play Mongolian chess with a friend. Learn the moves and play a short game.

immersePlan.name: Mark Naadam
immersePlan.text: Naadam is held on 11 to 13 July. Throw a small party with a game of strength, aim and speed.

immersePlan.name: Mark Tsagaan Sar
immersePlan.text: Tsagaan Sar, the White Moon, is the Mongolian new year. Visit an elder with a gift and greet them with the traditional gesture.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Orkhon Valley
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the grassy valley in central Mongolia with ancient inscriptions and the old capital of Kharkhorin. Imagine the herds.

immersePlan.name: Practise Tenger
immersePlan.text: Tenger is the eternal blue sky. Greet the sky before you do anything else today.

immersePlan.name: Practise ger
immersePlan.text: A ger is the round felt tent of the steppe. Think about what a home needs to be carried on a cart.

immersePlan.name: Practise anda
immersePlan.text: Anda is a sworn brother or sister, a bond closer than friendship. Spend time today with the person you would call your anda.

rules.why: Begin outside, with the horizon and the weather, before anything on a screen.
If you had to move camp tomorrow, what would you take? Keep little else.
Do what you said. The steppe has no contracts, only oaths.

rules.text: Feed the guest before you ask his business
rules.why: Anyone who comes to your door is given tea and food.
What is won together is divided fairly. Take your portion last if you lead.

rules.text: Respect every faith and quarrel with none
rules.why: Honour what others hold sacred, as the khans required.

read.title: The Secret History of the Mongols
read.creator: Anonymous, trans. Igor de Rachewiltz or Urgunge Onon
read.why: The Mongols’ own account of the rise of Chinggis Khan, written for the royal family. Part genealogy, part epic, blunt about fear, theft and murder. The only source from inside.

read.title: Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World
read.creator: Jack Weatherford
read.why: A warm and widely read retelling that argues for the empire’s contributions to trade, law and tolerance. Enthusiastic, and worth balancing with a more sober history.

read.title: The Mission of Friar William of Rubruck
read.creator: William of Rubruck, trans. Peter Jackson
read.why: A Flemish friar’s report of his journey to the court at Karakorum. Sharp-eyed about food, tents, drinking and a public debate between religions.

read.title: The Travels
read.creator: Marco Polo and Rustichello of Pisa
read.why: Seventeen years in the service of Khubilai Khan, dictated in a Genoese prison. Its account of the relay post and of paper money astonished Europe.

read.title: The Mongols
read.creator: David Morgan
read.why: The standard short history, careful with the evidence.

read.title: The Horde: How the Mongols Changed the World
read.creator: Marie Favereau
read.why: The western khanate on the Volga, seen from its own side as a lasting and inventive nomadic state.

watch.title: The Story of the Weeping Camel
watch.creator: Byambasuren Davaa and Luigi Falorni
watch.why: A Gobi family sends for a musician when a mother camel rejects her calf. A film made with a real family in their own ger.

watch.title: Mongol
watch.creator: Sergei Bodrov
watch.why: The early life of Temüjin, filmed on the steppe in Mongolian. Romantic, but the landscapes and the cold are true.

watch.title: The Cave of the Yellow Dog
watch.creator: Byambasuren Davaa
watch.why: A girl in a herding family finds a dog. Daily life, the moving of camp and the pull of the city, played by a real family.

watch.title: The Eagle Huntress
watch.creator: Otto Bell
watch.why: A thirteen-year-old Kazakh girl in western Mongolia trains a golden eagle. The Altai mountains in winter.

listen.title: Long songs
listen.creator: Namjilyn Norovbanzad
listen.why: Urtiin duu: a few words drawn out over minutes in huge slow arcs, with horse-head fiddle. Sung to the steppe, to horses and at weddings.

listen.title: Throat singing
listen.creator: Ensembles such as Altai Khairkhan and Egschiglen
listen.why: Khöömii: one singer holds a low drone and whistles a melody above it at the same time, in imitation of wind and water.

listen.title: Horse-head fiddle
listen.creator: Morin khuur players such as Chi Bulag
listen.why: Two strings of horsehair and a carved horse’s head. It can gallop, neigh and weep.

listen.title: Wrath of the Khans
listen.creator: Dan Carlin, Hardcore History
listen.why: Five long podcast episodes on the conquests that do not look away from what they cost.

art.title: Illustrations to the Compendium of Chronicles
art.creator: Workshop of Rashid al-Din, Tabriz
art.why: The first world history, written for the Mongol rulers of Iran. Its paintings show sieges, courts and enthronements in a style that joins Persian and Chinese. Leaves are in Edinburgh and the Khalili Collection.

art.title: Portraits of Chinggis and Khubilai Khan
art.creator: Yuan court painters
art.why: Half-length album portraits on silk in the National Palace Museum, Taipei. The source of every later image of the two men.

art.title: Khubilai Khan Hunting
art.creator: Liu Guandao
art.why: The khan in white ermine on a dark horse, with his consort Chabi and attendants from several lands, one of them drawing a bow at a bird.

art.title: A paiza
art.creator: Yuan dynasty workshop
art.why: An iron tablet inlaid with silver script reading: by the strength of Eternal Heaven, an edict of the Emperor. He who has no respect shall be guilty. One is in the Metropolitan Museum, New York.

eat.title: Boiled mutton
eat.creator: On the bone, in salted water, eaten with a knife
eat.why: The plain festive dish of the steppe. The fat is prized, and the guest of honour is given the shoulder blade.

eat.title: Buuz
eat.creator: Steamed dumplings of minced mutton and onion
eat.why: Made in their hundreds by every family for the lunar new year.

eat.title: Aaruul
eat.creator: Dried curds
eat.why: Sour, rock-hard and long-keeping. Soldiers carried it in their saddlebags.

eat.title: Khorkhog
eat.creator: Mutton cooked in a sealed can with hot stones
eat.why: The stones go in with the meat and cook it from inside. Afterwards the hot, greasy stones are passed from hand to hand for health.

drink.title: Suutei tsai
drink.creator: Tea boiled with milk and salt
drink.why: The first thing offered in any ger, ladled high to mix it. Sometimes with a spoonful of butter or millet.

drink.title: Airag
drink.creator: Fermented mare’s milk
drink.why: Summer’s drink, fizzy and sour, about as strong as weak beer. A guest is handed a full bowl.

drink.title: Black tea from a brick
drink.creator: Shaved from a pressed block
drink.why: Tea came to the steppe as bricks, which were also used as money.

customs.title: The threshold
customs.creator: Step over it, never on it
customs.why: To tread on the threshold of a ger was an insult to the household. At the court of the khans, guards stood by to enforce it, and envoys were warned.

customs.title: Passing with the right hand
customs.creator: Left hand under the right elbow
customs.why: Give and receive food and drink with the right hand or both hands, sleeves rolled down. Take at least a sip.

customs.title: Circling the ovoo
customs.creator: Three times, with the sun
customs.why: At a cairn on a pass, walk round it clockwise, add a stone and perhaps a little milk, and continue.

customs.title: Respect for the fire and for water
customs.creator: Nothing unclean in either
customs.why: Do not put rubbish in the hearth, point a knife at it or stretch your feet towards it. The old law forbade washing in running streams.

games.title: Shagai
games.creator: Game of ankle bones · Mongolia
games.why: Sheep ankle bones land on one of four sides, called horse, camel, sheep and goat. They are flicked, thrown, raced and used to tell fortunes.

games.title: Bökh
games.creator: Wrestling · Mongolia
games.why: Wrestlers in open jackets and boots enter with an eagle dance. A bout ends when any part of the body above the knee touches the ground.

games.title: Shatar
games.creator: Mongolian chess
games.why: Played with carved camels for bishops and carts for rooks. The queen is a guard dog or a tiger.

games.title: Archery
games.creator: Sport · Mongolia
games.why: At Naadam, men and women shoot blunt arrows at a low wall of small leather rings, and the judges sing out the hits.

festivals.title: Naadam
festivals.creator: 11 to 13 July
festivals.why: The national games: wrestling, archery and long-distance races ridden by children. Held in the capital and in every district.

festivals.title: Tsagaan Sar
festivals.creator: The lunar new year, in January or February
festivals.why: The White Moon. Families visit their elders in order of age, greet them by supporting their forearms, and eat dumplings and white foods.

festivals.title: Chinggis Khaan’s birthday
festivals.creator: The first day of the first month of winter, in November
festivals.why: A public holiday in Mongolia since 2012. The nine white banners are honoured.

places.title: Kharkhorin
places.creator: Övörkhangai, Mongolia
places.why: The site of Karakorum, the imperial capital. Little remains but stone tortoises and a good museum. Beside it stands Erdene Zuu, a monastery built from its ruins in 1586.

places.title: Burkhan Khaldun
places.creator: Khentii, Mongolia
places.why: The mountain where the young Temüjin hid from his enemies and which he vowed to honour every morning. A World Heritage Site in a strictly protected area. Permits are needed.

places.title: Chinggis Khaan National Museum
places.creator: Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia
places.why: Opened in 2022, with nine floors on the steppe empires from the Xiongnu onwards.

places.title: The equestrian statue at Tsonjin Boldog
places.creator: Töv, Mongolia
places.why: A forty-metre steel Chinggis Khan on horseback, an hour east of the capital. You can stand on the horse’s head.

places.title: The Orkhon Valley
places.creator: Central Mongolia
places.why: Grassland along the river that was the heart of steppe empires for a thousand years. Stay with a herding family through a community tourism group.

places.title: The site of Xanadu
places.creator: Zhenglan Banner, Inner Mongolia, China
places.why: The grass-grown walls of Shangdu, Khubilai’s summer capital, which Marco Polo described and Coleridge dreamed of.

ethics.title: Loyalty
ethics.text: Chinggis Khan rewarded those who stayed true to their own lords, even his enemies, and executed those who betrayed them to him.
ethics.practice: Stand by someone today when it would be easier not to.

ethics.title: Keeping one’s word
ethics.text: An oath is the whole of the law between free riders.
ethics.practice: Make no promise today that you will not keep exactly.

ethics.title: Hospitality
ethics.text: The guest is fed and sheltered, whoever he is.
ethics.practice: Give your best food to a visitor.

ethics.title: Merit
ethics.text: Commanders were chosen for ability. A herdsman could lead ten thousand.
ethics.practice: Give credit today to the person who earned it, not the person who outranks them.

ethics.title: Frugality
ethics.text: The khan wore what his herdsmen wore and distrusted luxury as the ruin of nations.
ethics.practice: Go without one comfort you take for granted.

ethics.title: Respect for all faiths
ethics.text: Priests of every religion were freed from tax and asked to pray for the khan. No one was to be persecuted for belief.
ethics.practice: Learn one thing today about a faith that is not yours, from someone who holds it.

philosophy.title: The Eternal Sky
philosophy.text: Above every people and every creed is one heaven, which grants fortune to those in harmony with it. The Mongols prayed to it directly, on high ground.
philosophy.practice: Stand under the open sky for five minutes and ask what it asks of you.

philosophy.title: The bound arrows
philosophy.text: One shaft snaps. Five together do not. The founding story of the nation is a lesson in unity.
philosophy.practice: Whom do you need to be bound with?

philosophy.title: A people is its people
philosophy.text: A nomad realm is the folk who follow, not a stretch of land. Loyalty has to be earned and kept, or they ride away.
philosophy.practice: What holds the people in your life to you?

philosophy.title: Movement
philosophy.text: To stay in one place is to exhaust it. Health, for land and for people, lies in moving on at the right time.
philosophy.practice: What have you stayed in too long?

philosophy.title: Different fingers, one hand
philosophy.text: Möngke Khan told a missionary that God has given different ways to different peoples. The court set the religions to debate instead of fight.
philosophy.practice: Hold two rival views in your hand today without closing it.

philosophy.title: Won on horseback
philosophy.text: Conquest and government are different skills. The Mongols learned to borrow administrators from the peoples they had beaten.
philosophy.practice: What did you win by force that you now need other gifts to keep?

philosophy.title: The price
philosophy.text: The same armies that opened the roads from China to Europe destroyed cities and killed on a scale not seen before. Both are true.
philosophy.practice: What good in your life has a cost someone else paid?

philosophy.title: Fortune
philosophy.text: Chinggis Khan believed heaven had chosen him, and also that he must not grow soft. Luck is given, and must be deserved daily.
philosophy.practice: What luck have you had, and what have you done to deserve it?

journal: What did you carry today that you did not need?
What did the sky look like this morning?
How far did you go?
What did you read from the land?
Whom did you feed?
Whose hospitality did you accept, and how well?
What promise did you keep?
Who are your sworn companions?
Whom have you bound yourself to?
Where are you one arrow alone?
What did you share, and did you take your portion last?
What have you stayed in too long?
What would you take if you moved camp tomorrow?
What did your body learn today?
Whom did you honour for merit?
What luxury is softening you?
What does your homeland mean to you?
Who are your ancestors, seven generations back?
What story did you tell at the fire?
What did you decide alone that should have gone to council?
Whose faith did you respect today?
What did you win that you do not know how to keep?
Who paid for something you enjoy?
What threshold did you tread on?
What winter are you preparing for?
When did you last sleep under the sky?
What is your horse: the thing that carries you?
What fortune have you been given?
What have you done to deserve it?

reflect: What did greeting the sky each morning change?
What do you now own less of?
Whose door did you open, and who opened theirs?
What can your body do that it could not before?
Which habit of the steppe will you keep?

intro: In the twelfth century the peoples of the Mongolian steppe were herders of horses, sheep, goats, cattle and camels, living in felt tents and moving with the seasons. They were divided into feuding tribes, and the settled empires to the south paid one to fight another. Into this world, around 1162, a boy named Temüjin was born to a minor chief. When he was nine his father was poisoned by enemies and the clan abandoned the widow and her children to starve. They survived on roots, fish and marmots. Temüjin was captured and enslaved, escaped, and slowly gathered followers who came to him for his ability, not his birth.

By 1206 he had defeated or absorbed every tribe on the steppe. A great assembly on the Onon river gave him the title Chinggis Khan. He then did something new. He broke up the old tribes and reorganised the whole people into units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand, commanded by men he chose for merit and loyalty. He had a script adopted, laws recorded and a guard formed that served as a school for officers. The nation he made was an army, and the army was a nation.

What followed was the largest land empire in history. In twenty years Chinggis Khan’s armies took northern China and overran Central Asia and Iran. Under his sons and grandsons they conquered Russia, reached Hungary and Poland, destroyed Baghdad, and completed the conquest of China, where his grandson Khubilai founded the Yuan dynasty. At its height the empire ran from the Pacific to the Danube.

The conquests were terrible. Cities that resisted were destroyed and their people killed or driven before the army. Parts of Iran and Central Asia took centuries to recover. A survivor of Bukhara summed it up in six verbs: they came, they sapped, they burnt, they slew, they plundered and they departed.

Yet once the wars were over the Mongols held the roads of Eurasia open as no one had before. A system of relay stations carried couriers and envoys across the continent. Merchants, craftsmen, doctors and astronomers moved under the khans’ protection, and with them went paper money, gunpowder, printing, noodles and new medicine. The rulers taxed lightly, promoted foreigners, and required that every religion be left in peace: a Flemish friar found Christians, Muslims, Buddhists and Daoists debating at the court of Karakorum by the khan’s command. The plague travelled the same roads in the 1340s, and the empire’s successor states weakened and fell one by one.

The culture that produced all this was never only an army. It was, and is, a way of living lightly on a hard land: the round tent that goes up in an hour, the hearth that must be kept clean, the tea poured for any stranger, the oath that is kept, the morning milk flicked to the sky. About a quarter of Mongolia’s people still herd. This Onda follows that older, quieter pattern, and keeps the conquests in view as history, with their price.
guide.origin: The grasslands of Mongolia, and from there to Korea, Hungary, Syria and Vietnam
guide.era: Temüjin was proclaimed Chinggis Khan in 1206. The Mongols were driven from China in 1368. The steppe way of life continues

figures.name: Chinggis Khan
figures.bio: Born Temüjin. Founder of the Mongol nation and empire. He could not read, forbade the use of his name and image, and was buried in a place still unknown.

figures.name: Hoelun
figures.bio: His mother, who kept five children alive after the clan left them. The Secret History gives her some of its fiercest speeches.

figures.name: Börte
figures.bio: His first wife, betrothed to him in childhood, kidnapped and recovered. Mother of the four sons who inherited the empire, and his counsellor.

figures.name: Jamukha
figures.bio: His sworn brother and then his great rival for the steppe. Defeated at last, he asked for a death without bloodshed and was given it.

figures.name: Subutai
figures.bio: A blacksmith’s son who became the greatest of the generals, directing campaigns from China to Hungary.

figures.name: Ögedei Khan
figures.bio: The third son and second great khan. Genial and a heavy drinker, he built Karakorum and the relay post.

figures.name: Sorghaghtani Beki
figures.bio: A Christian princess, widow of the youngest son. She ran her own lands, educated her four sons in different traditions and saw two of them become great khans.

figures.name: Yelü Chucai
figures.bio: A Khitan scholar taken into service after the fall of Beijing. He persuaded the Mongols to tax northern China instead of turning it into pasture.

figures.name: Möngke Khan
figures.bio: Grandson of Chinggis and the last ruler of a united empire. Austere and capable.

figures.name: Khubilai Khan
figures.bio: Grandson who conquered southern China, founded the Yuan dynasty and built a capital on the site of Beijing. Marco Polo’s patron.

figures.name: Khutulun
figures.bio: A great-great-granddaughter of Chinggis who rode to war with her father and, by Marco Polo’s account, would marry only a man who could out-wrestle her. None did.

figures.name: Rashid al-Din
figures.bio: Physician and vizier to the Mongol rulers of Iran, who wrote for them a history of all the peoples of the known world.

history.detail: On the Onon river, clutching a clot of blood in his fist, as the story has it. His father dies about nine years later.
At the head of the Onon the united tribes raise a white banner with nine tails and proclaim him Chinggis Khan.
The Jin empire is invaded. Its capital, on the site of modern Beijing, falls in 1215.
After a governor murders a Mongol trade caravan, the Khwarazmian empire is destroyed. Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv and Nishapur are sacked.
He dies in August while besieging the Tangut kingdom. His body is taken home and buried in secret.
Ögedei builds a walled capital on the Orkhon, with a palace, quarters for craftsmen and merchants and places of worship for several faiths.
Batu and Subutai conquer the Russian principalities and, in April 1241, defeat Polish and Hungarian armies within two days. News of Ögedei’s death turns them back.
Möngke Khan orders Christians, Muslims and Buddhists to argue their cases before judges. William of Rubruck takes part and records it.
Hülegü’s army takes the city of the caliphs after a short siege. The slaughter and the loss of its libraries are remembered across the Muslim world.
An Egyptian army defeats a Mongol force in Palestine. In the same year civil war over the succession splits the empire into four realms.
Khubilai proclaims a Chinese-style dynasty and completes the conquest of the Song. For the first time in centuries all China has one ruler.
Two seaborne invasions fail, the second wrecked by a typhoon the Japanese call the divine wind.
The Black Death spreads along the trade routes from Central Asia to the Black Sea and on into Europe and the Middle East.
A Chinese rebel founds the Ming dynasty and the last Yuan emperor rides north to the steppe, where the Mongols continue under their own khans.

concepts.detail: The Mongols held that the Eternal Blue Sky had given Chinggis Khan and his line the mandate to rule the world. Submission was obedience to heaven, and resistance was rebellion.
Every man from fifteen to seventy belonged to a unit that mixed the old tribes. No one could leave his unit, and the ten answered for each of its members.
Rulings on military discipline, the great hunt, theft of livestock, the treatment of envoys and the division of booty. Known only from quotations by others.
Stations every forty kilometres or so, supplied by the local people. Envoys with a tablet of authority changed horses and rode on.
The princes and commanders gathered to acclaim a new khan and settle great matters. Its decisions bound those who came.
Clergy of all faiths were exempt from tax and labour service and were asked to pray for the ruler. It kept subject peoples quiet and hedged heaven’s bets.
The century in which a single power kept the routes between China and the Mediterranean open and safe. Later writers said a girl could carry a gold dish across it unharmed.
After 1260: the Yuan in China and Mongolia, the Ilkhanate in Iran, the Chaghatai realm in Central Asia and the Golden Horde on the western steppe.

concepts.term: The white and the black banner
concepts.detail: The spirit banner of white horsehair stood before the khan’s tent in peacetime. The black one went to war. Both held the fortune of the nation.

facts.text: A Mongol soldier travelled with three or four spare horses and could live for days on dried curd and mare’s milk.
The empire at its height covered about twenty-four million square kilometres.
Women managed the camps, the herds and the trade while the men were at war, and several widows ruled the empire as regents.
The Mongolian vertical script was adapted from Uyghur writing in the time of Chinggis Khan and is still used in Inner Mongolia.
Khubilai’s government issued paper money that had to be accepted on pain of death.
Mongolia today has about three and a half million people and some seventy million head of livestock.

sensitivity.note: The Mongol Empire was built by conquest that killed millions. The culture behind it is the living heritage of Mongolians today. This Onda borrows the daily customs of the steppe, which are older and gentler than the empire, and reports the conquests plainly.
requiredCaveats: The Mongol conquests destroyed cities and populations across Asia and eastern Europe. Admiration for the empire’s order should not hide that.
The offering to the sky and the respect for hearth and cairn are living religious customs in Mongolia. Do them simply, as a guest would, or leave them out.
Chinggis Khan is a national founder to Mongolians and a destroyer in the memory of Iranians, Arabs, Russians and Chinese. Both views are held by people alive now.
